title: Annuities and Perpetuities
summary: Shortcuts for valuing a stream of identical payments, instead of discounting each one by hand.

lesson.body:
You already know how to discount one cash flow. Now suppose there are forty of them, all the same size, arriving at regular intervals — a lease, a bond's coupons, a management fee, a pension payment. Discounting each one separately works, but it is forty lines of arithmetic for a pattern that has a closed-form answer.

A stream of equal payments at equal intervals is an [[annuity]]. If it never ends, it is a [[perpetuity]]. Both have one-line formulas, and both are worth recognising on sight — the moment you see "the same amount, every period", you should stop reaching for a column of discount factors.

The annuity formula looks arbitrary until you see where it comes from: it is a geometric series. Each payment is worth the previous one divided by (1+r), so the terms shrink by a constant ratio, and geometric series collapse into a single expression.

The [[perpetuity]] case is the one worth internalising, because it is almost embarrassingly simple: **PV = PMT / r**. At a 5% [[discount-rate]], a payment of $1 forever is worth $20 today. Not $50, not infinity — $20.

That surprises people, and the reason it should not is [[compounding]] running in reverse. The payment in year 100 is worth almost nothing today, so the far tail of "forever" contributes almost nothing to the total. Infinity in the numerator does not produce infinity in the answer, because the discount factor shrinks faster than the payments accumulate.

lesson.plainReading: Present value equals the payment, multiplied by one minus the discount factor for the final period, all divided by the rate. The fraction is often called the annuity factor — it is simply the sum of all the individual [[discount-factor|discount factors]] rolled into one number.

variables.meaning: the payment made each period — identical every time, which is what makes it an [[annuity]]

lesson.plainReading: Present value of a payment that never stops equals the payment divided by the rate. This is the annuity formula with n pushed to infinity, at which point the discount factor term vanishes.

lesson.body: A fund will pay you $2,000 at the end of each year for the next ten years. Your [[required-return]] is 7%.
walkthrough: **The annuity factor.** (1 - 1.07^-10) / 0.07. Since 1.07^10 = 1.9672, its reciprocal is 0.5083, so the numerator is 1 - 0.5083 = 0.4917. Divide by 0.07: **7.0236**.

Sanity check the size of that factor. Ten payments discounted at 7% are worth about 7.0 times one payment — less than 10, obviously, but not dramatically less. That ratio is a quick way to catch an error: if your annuity factor exceeds n, you have made a mistake.

**Now shift the timing.** If those payments arrive at the *start* of each year instead — an [[annuity-due]] — every payment sits one period closer to today, so multiply the whole thing by 1.07: $14,047.16 x 1.07 = **$15,030.46**.

That timing change is worth $983.30, about 7% of the value. On a $2,000 payment stream it is a rounding error; on a large fee stream it is a real number, and it is decided entirely by whether payments land at the beginning or the end of the period.

lesson.body:
**The formula assumes the first payment arrives one period from now.** That is an *ordinary* annuity. If the first payment is today — rent, insurance premiums, most subscription arrangements — you have an [[annuity-due]], and every payment is one period closer, so the value is higher by exactly a factor of (1+r).

Spreadsheet functions make this easy to get wrong, because the timing argument is optional and defaults to ordinary. If a valuation looks about 5-10% low and the cash flows arrive at period start, check that argument before you check anything else.

The perpetuity formula is the one you will actually reach for, usually without calling it that.

**Terminal values.** Almost every discounted cash flow model ends with "and then it grows steadily forever", valued as a growing perpetuity. A large share of the answer typically sits in that one term, which is why small changes to the assumed long-run rate move valuations so much.

**Fee streams.** A management fee on committed capital is an annuity in all but name. Valuing what a fund's fee stream is worth to the manager is an annuity calculation, and it is a useful sanity check when someone describes a fee as "only" a certain percentage.

**Real assets.** Infrastructure concessions, ground rents and long leases are close to textbook annuities, which is exactly why they are described as bond-like and why they reprice so sharply when [[discount-rate|discount rates]] move.

items: Equal payments at equal intervals is an annuity; forever is a perpetuity. Recognise the pattern and stop discounting by hand.
PV of a perpetuity is simply PMT / r. At 5%, a dollar forever is worth twenty dollars today.
The annuity factor must be less than the number of payments. If it is not, you have made an error.
Ordinary annuity pays at period end; annuity due pays at the start and is worth (1+r) times as much.

questions.stem: What is the present value of $2,000 received at the end of each year for 10 years, discounted at 7% a year?
questions.inputHint: Answer in dollars. Do not type a $ sign.
questions.explanation: The annuity factor is (1 - 1.07^-10)/0.07 = 7.0236. Multiply by $2,000 to get $14,047.16. Note the factor is below 10 — it must be, since later payments are worth less than the first.

questions.stem: You invest $500 at the end of every quarter for 5 years. The rate is 8% a year, compounded quarterly. What is the value at the end?
questions.inputHint: Answer in dollars. Convert the rate and the periods to quarters first.
questions.explanation: One period is a quarter, so r = 0.02 and n = 20. FV = 500 x ((1.02^20 - 1)/0.02) = 500 x 24.297 = $12,148.68. The most common wrong answer uses r = 0.08 with n = 20, which applies 8% per quarter and badly overstates the result.

questions.stem: An infrastructure asset is expected to pay $50,000 a year indefinitely. At a 6% discount rate, what is it worth today?
questions.inputHint: Answer in dollars, to the nearest dollar.
questions.explanation: PV = PMT / r = 50,000 / 0.06 = $833,333. A payment forever is worth a finite amount, because the far-future payments discount to almost nothing.

questions.stem: Two identical payment streams differ only in timing: one pays at the end of each period, the other at the start. How do their present values compare?
choices: The start-of-period stream is worth (1+r) times as much
They are worth the same, since the payments and the number of periods are identical
The start-of-period stream is worth one extra payment more
The end-of-period stream is worth more, because the money has longer to compound
rationales: Correct. Every payment sits exactly one period closer to today, so the whole stream is discounted one period less — a uniform multiplication by (1+r).
Timing is not a detail here. The same dollars arriving earlier are worth more, which is the entire subject of the previous topic.
Tempting, and wrong. The difference is a proportional (1+r) uplift on the whole stream, not the addition of one payment. Those coincide only in special cases.
This confuses the investor's position with the payer's. Receiving money later is worse for you, not better — there is nothing to compound until it arrives.
questions.explanation: An annuity due is an ordinary annuity shifted one period earlier, so its value is exactly (1+r) times as large. In the worked example that shift was worth $983 on a $14,047 stream.

questions.stem: "A payment stream that never ends must be worth an infinite amount today." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — the discount factor shrinks geometrically, so distant payments contribute almost nothing and the total converges
False — because no asset in practice actually lasts forever
True — an infinite number of positive payments must sum to infinity
False — because the discount rate would have to be zero for the sum to be finite
rationales: Correct. At 6%, the payment in year 100 is worth about 0.3% of its face value, and year 200 is worth almost literally nothing. The series converges to PMT / r.
Practically true, but it is not the reason. Even a genuinely infinite stream has a finite present value, which is the point being tested.
This is the misconception. An infinite sum of *shrinking* terms can be finite — that is what a convergent geometric series is.
Backwards. A discount rate of zero is precisely the case where the sum *would* be infinite. A positive rate is what makes it converge.
questions.explanation: The perpetuity result is the clearest demonstration that discounting is exponential. Because each payment is worth a constant fraction of the last, the series converges — and it converges to something small enough to be surprising.

questions.stem: An analyst computes an annuity factor of 12.4 for a 10-year annuity at 6%. What should you conclude?
choices: The factor is plausible, since 10 payments at 6% compound to more than 10
The calculation is wrong — an annuity factor can never exceed the number of payments
The factor is plausible if the annuity is an annuity due
The factor is plausible only if the rate is applied monthly
rationales: This confuses present value with future value. An annuity *factor* is a sum of discount factors, each below 1, so it cannot exceed the count of payments.
Correct. Each of the 10 discount factors is less than 1, so their sum must be under 10. The right answer is about 7.36. This is the cheapest sanity check in the whole topic.
An annuity due multiplies by 1.06, giving about 7.8 — still nowhere near 12.4, and still below 10.
Monthly compounding changes the periodic rate but the factor is still a sum of sub-1 discount factors over 10 payments. The ceiling holds.
questions.explanation: Annuity factor < n, always, for any positive rate. Carrying that one inequality in your head catches a large share of spreadsheet errors instantly.

questions.stem: A valuation model projects five years of cash flow explicitly, then a growing perpetuity thereafter. The analyst raises the long-run growth rate from 2% to 3%, with a 7% discount rate. What happens to the terminal value?
choices: It rises by roughly 1%, matching the change in the growth assumption
It rises by roughly 25%, because the denominator falls from 5% to 4%
It is unchanged, since the explicit forecast period is unaffected
It falls, because a higher growth rate raises the required return
rationales: The change in the assumption is 1 percentage point, but the *effect* is not 1% — the growth rate sits in the denominator alongside the discount rate, where a small change is amplified.
Correct. A growing perpetuity is PMT/(r-g). The denominator goes from 0.07-0.02 = 0.05 to 0.07-0.03 = 0.04, so the value rises by 0.05/0.04 = 1.25, about 25%.
The explicit period is unaffected, but the terminal value is not — and in most models the terminal value is the majority of the answer.
There is no mechanical link from growth to the discount rate here, and the direction is wrong regardless: faster growth makes a stream more valuable.
questions.explanation: This is why terminal value assumptions get so much scrutiny. Because r and g both live in the denominator, and (r-g) is a small number, modest changes to either produce large changes in value. Note that as g approaches r the formula breaks down entirely — a growth rate at or above the discount rate implies infinite value, which is a sign the model is being asked something unreasonable.
questions.reviewNote: The growing perpetuity formula PMT/(r-g) is introduced here only in a question, not in the lesson body. Verify I have not skipped a step you would want taught explicitly — it may deserve its own lesson block or a dedicated topic.
